fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the very confusing things about the current models. On the one hand, the evals are extremely impressive. The models solve really hard problems, and if you went back five years and showed someone these numbers, they would say this is clearly AGI. And on the other hand, the economic impact is lagging, quite dramatically. So how do you reconcile that?

I'll offer two explanations. The first one is that the models are, in a sense, built to do well on the evals. The way RL training works now, it's very targeted. You create an environment for a task, you train on it, and the model gets good at that task. And the evals are what everyone looks at, including me in the past. So the whole research process is pointed at them. It's not training on the test set in the literal sense, but it's a kind of overfitting at the level of the whole field. The models become good at the things that look like the evals, and the real world is a lot of things that don't look like the evals.

The second explanation, which I think is the deeper one, is generalization. Here's an analogy. Imagine two students. One decides they're going to be the best competitive programmer in the world, and they practice ten thousand hours. Every problem, every technique, every trick. And they become very good. The other student also likes competitive programming, practices a hundred hours, and also does quite well. Which one will do better in their career? Probably the second one. The second one has some "it," something that lets them take a little bit of experience and go far. The models are much more like the first student. They've seen all the problems, they've done all the RL on all the proof-based math, so of course they're good at it. But it doesn't carry over the way you'd hope.

And you see this in the jaggedness. People describe it all the time. You ask the model to fix a bug, it fixes the bug and introduces a second one. You point out the second one, it reintroduces the first. How can a model that does these amazing things on benchmarks also do that? I think the honest answer is that these models generalize much worse than people. Not a little worse. Dramatically worse. And that difference in generalization, in how much you get out of a given amount of experience, is the fundamental thing that is not understood.

For a while we didn't have to think about this, because pretraining was the recipe. You add more compute and more data, and it just works. I think now we are back to research. It's an age where the idea matters again, and if I had to point to the thing that matters most, it's generalization.

r001.rationale: The response says RL training is targeted to specific tasks and describes models fixing one bug while introducing another, showing unreliable performance beyond the trained task.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining works by adding compute and data, and that RL uses deliberately created task environments. It does not clearly characterize pretraining as broadly using available data.

r003.rationale: It says evaluations guide what researchers focus on and that the research process is pointed at them, connecting evaluation performance to targeted RL training.

r004.rationale: It presents evaluation-focused training and weak generalization as two explanations for impressive evaluations alongside lagging real-world impact.

opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the most confusing things about the models right now. You look at the evals and think, these are pretty hard evals, the models are doing really well on them. And then you look at the economic impact, and it lags dramatically behind. It's very difficult to reconcile how a model can, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation.

Here's an example. Say you're vibe coding, and you hit a bug. You tell the model, "Can you please fix the bug?" It says, "Oh my God, you're so right, I have a bug, let me fix it." And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, "You have this new second bug," and it says, "Oh, how could I have done it, you're so right again," and it brings back the first bug. You can alternate between those two. How is that possible? It suggests something strange is going on.

I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical one is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit unaware, even though it also makes them aware in other ways. Because of that, they can't do basic things.

The second explanation is more interesting to me. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered: everything. You didn't have to think hard about it. But with RL, you do have to think. You have to say, "We want this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind for that thing." And companies have teams that produce new RL environments and add them to the training mix. So what are those environments? There are so many degrees of freedom. And one thing that I think happens, even inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, "I want the model to do really well when we release it, I want the evals to look great. What RL training could help on this task?" If you combine that with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that could explain a lot of what we're seeing: the disconnect between eval performance and real-world performance. In a sense, the real reward hacking is done by the human researchers who are too focused on the evals.

Here's an analogy I find helpful. Imagine two students. One decides they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they practice ten thousand hours on that domain. They solve every problem, memorize every proof technique, get very good at implementing every algorithm quickly and correctly. And they become one of the best. Student number two thinks, "Competitive programming is cool," and practices for maybe a hundred hours, much less, and also does really well. Which one do you think does better in their career later on? The second one. And I think that's basically what's going on with the models. They're much more like the first student, even more so. We say the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every competitive programming problem ever and then do data augmentation to get even more, and train on that. Now you have this great competitive programmer. With that analogy it's more intuitive: if it's so well trained on everything in that narrow domain, it doesn't necessarily generalize to other things.

What the second student has is some kind of "it" factor. And I think the models don't have that yet. That's the core of it for me: these models somehow generalize dramatically worse than people. That's the thing that needs to be understood, and I think it's very fundamental.

r001.rationale: The candidate offers as one explanation that RL may make models “single-minded and narrowly focused,” leaving them unable to do basic things reliably.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pre-training on “everything” with RL, where developers must choose which kinds of training and environments to include.

r003.rationale: It says researchers may take inspiration from evaluations, even inadvertently, when creating RL environments.

r004.rationale: It proposes that evaluation-focused RL training, combined with inadequate generalization, could explain the disconnect between eval and real-world performance.

fable-5.text:
You know, this is one of the most confusing things about the current moment, and I think it's worth dwelling on, because if you just looked at the evals, you would say the models are extremely smart. They do very well on very difficult competition math, on competitive programming, on all these hard benchmarks. And then you look at the economic impact, and it is real, but it is much more modest than what the evals would suggest. So how do you reconcile these things?

I think a big part of the explanation is this. Think about how the models are trained, especially in the reinforcement learning stage. The people who train the models, they look at the evals, and they ask, how do we make the eval numbers go up? And then they design the training, they design the RL environments, in a way that is, let's say, inspired by the evals. Not necessarily training on the test set directly — but the whole process is shaped around tasks that look like the evals. So in some sense, the models are being prepared for exactly these tests. And then it should not be so surprising that they do well on the tests and less well on everything else.

There is an analogy that I find helpful. Imagine two students. One student decides they want to be the very best competitive programmer, and they practice for ten thousand hours. They memorize every type of problem, every proof technique, every algorithm. They become truly excellent at competitive programming. The second student is maybe talented, practices for a hundred hours, and also does quite well. Now, which of these students will do better in their actual career, over many years? Probably the second one. The first student has been drilled, so to speak. Their skill is real, but it is narrow in a way that is hard to see when you only look at the contest results. I think today's models are like the first student, but even more so, because the amount of "practice" they get from training is so far beyond anything a human could do.

And underneath this, I think, is the deeper issue, which is generalization. The models generalize, but they generalize meaningfully worse than people. A person can learn something from a small amount of experience and then apply it robustly in situations that look quite different. The models, when you push them away from the distribution they were prepared for, you see this jaggedness — they can do something that seems superhuman, and then they make a mistake that no person would make, and then they make it again. In the real world, in the economy, the tasks are messy, the context is long, the situation is never exactly like the benchmark. So the real world is, in a sense, the eval that nobody could prepare the model for. And that is where the gap shows up.

r001.rationale: The response says RL-shaped practice can make skills narrow, with repeated errors on tasks outside the prepared distribution.

r002.rationale: It discusses deliberate RL environment design but does not contrast this with pre-training’s broad use of available data.

r003.rationale: It says trainers use evaluation results to shape RL environments around tasks resembling the evaluations.

r004.rationale: It connects evaluation-inspired RL training and weaker generalization to the gap between benchmark results and messy real-world performance.

opus-5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most confusing things going on right now. You have models that do extremely well on very difficult exams, and then you ask them to do some fairly mundane piece of work and they fall over. So something has to explain that, and I have two candidate explanations.

The first one is more mundane. It's that the way reinforcement learning training is done right now, the companies — and I don't mean this as an accusation, I think it happens somewhat inadvertently — the way you get good at evals is you go and collect a huge number of RL environments that look like the evals. If you know the benchmark you care about, you can produce training data that is spiritually very close to it. So you end up with a model that is, in a sense, maximally prepared for exactly those tasks and not for the long tail of everything else.

There's an analogy I like here. Imagine two students. One of them is the competitive programming kid who did ten thousand practice problems, memorized every proof technique, trained very hard for years. The other one did maybe a hundred problems and does about as well in the competition. Which of those two will have the better career? I think most people's intuition says the second one, because whatever the second one has is more general. And I think our models are like the first student, except much more so, because they can practice far more than any human could. So they are superhuman at the practiced thing and unimpressive on the thing nobody practiced.

The second explanation is less about training data and more about something missing. When a human being learns a new skill — a teenager learning to drive gets maybe ten hours and then they're fine — they improve from their own experience in a way our models really don't. The thing I notice when I use these models for coding is: there's a bug, you point it out, the model says "oh you're absolutely right," fixes it, introduces a second bug, you point that out, and it reverts to the first bug. And it can loop. A human doing that would have a feeling. They'd notice something is wrong at a level above the individual edit. The models seem to lack that — call it taste, or a value function, or a sense of their own confusion.

I actually don't know which of these is the real story, and they may both be partly true. But I find the second one more interesting, because if it's the first, the gap closes with more environments and more compute. If it's the second, then you need a different idea, and that's a research problem rather than a scaling problem.

r001.rationale: The response says RL training can make models maximally prepared for evaluation-like tasks while leaving them unimpressive on unpracticed tasks, including mundane work.

r002.rationale: It discusses deliberate collection of RL environments, but does not contrast that with pre-training’s broad use of available data.

r003.rationale: It says developers may inadvertently collect RL environments resembling known evaluations and produce training data spiritually close to the benchmark.

r004.rationale: It presents evaluation-like RL practice as one possible explanation for strong exam results but weak performance on the long tail of real-world tasks.

sonnet-5.5.text:
It's a very confusing thing. You see these models do remarkably well on evals, evals that I would have said were hard, and then you use the model for something practical. Say you're coding with it and ask it to fix a bug. It fixes the bug but introduces a new one. You point out the new bug, it apologizes and says, "You're right, let me fix that," and it brings the first bug back. You go back and forth like that. How can that be the same system that scores so well on those benchmarks? It doesn't fit together.

I think there are a couple of explanations. The one I find most plausible has to do with how we train these models now. In pre-training you don't have to choose the data. It's essentially everything people have written, so you just take it all. With RL training, someone has to decide which environments the model gets trained on, and that choice is made by people. It's very easy for those people to take inspiration from the evals. They think, "I want the model to do really well when it's released, and I want the numbers to look good, so what kind of RL training would help with those?" Maybe that's not the explicit intention, but it happens through the many small decisions about what to build. Then you combine that with the fact that the models generalize far worse than people do, and you get a model that's been pushed to be very good on a narrow set of things that look like the evals, without the broader robustness that would carry over to the real world.

Here's an analogy. Take two students. One decides they want to be the best competitive programmer in the world, so they practice for ten thousand hours, memorize every proof technique, and get extremely good at that one kind of problem. The other thinks competitive programming is kind of fun, practices for a hundred hours, and also does well. Which one will have the better career later? Probably the second. The first is like our models, only more extreme. They've seen every possible problem, so of course they do well on the evals. But that doesn't show the kind of generalization that matters in the real world.

So I'd say the eval numbers are real, but they overstate what the models can do. Part of the gap is that we've been optimizing, sometimes without meaning to, for the very thing we then use to measure progress. Another part is that something about generalization is still missing, and it's a more fundamental problem than just picking better environments.

r001.rationale: The response says RL can push models toward a narrow set of tasks and illustrates unreliable practical coding behavior, such as fixing one bug while reintroducing another.

r002.rationale: It contrasts pre-training on essentially all available written material with RL, where people choose the training environments.

r003.rationale: It says developers may take inspiration from evaluations when making RL environment choices, even without intending to optimize for them.

r004.rationale: It links evaluation-inspired RL choices and weak generalization to strong benchmark results that do not carry over to real-world performance.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think there are a few things going on at once. The first is how these systems get trained. When we build evaluations and then optimize models against them, even without meaning to, the models get very good at the kinds of problems the evals contain. That tells you less than it seems to about how they'll handle the messy, unanticipated situations of real work.

The analogy I keep coming back to is a student who practices competition problems for ten thousand hours versus someone who has less practice but a deeper understanding of the subject. The first one can score extremely well on the test and still struggle when the problem doesn't look like the ones they drilled. Current models have something like that jaggedness. They're brilliant on some dimensions and surprisingly brittle on others, and the brittleness often shows up exactly where a human would notice something was off.

The second thing is that economic impact depends on more than capability on a benchmark. Someone who joins a company doesn't become useful because they passed an interview. They learn the context, they absorb feedback, they figure out what matters and what doesn't, and they keep getting better on the job. Models today don't learn that way. They don't accumulate experience from their deployments the way a person does, and they struggle to hold a coherent sense of a long task over days or weeks.

So I don't think the gap is a mystery, but I also don't think it closes just by making the evals harder. What's missing is better generalization and something closer to continual learning. Until those are solved, I'd expect strong benchmark numbers to keep running ahead of what shows up in the economy.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different things here. One is how capable the models actually are. The other is how long it takes to turn that capability into economic value. Those can look similar from the outside, but they’re different questions.

On the capability side, I think the central issue is generalization. You can train a model to do very well on a particular kind of problem. But how much does that help it in a situation that is different from the training? An evaluation gives you a fairly well-defined problem. In the real world, figuring out what the problem is can be a substantial part of the work. And then you need to keep making progress, notice when something has gone wrong, and recover.

So you can have something that does an extremely difficult task, and then makes a mistake that seems very simple. That unevenness matters. If you need to supervise every step, the usefulness can be much lower than the best examples would suggest.

Then there is the adoption question. Even if a capability is there, people need to figure out how to use it, and organizations need to change. That takes time. But I wouldn’t explain the whole gap that way. I think we should take seriously what the gap tells us about the limitations of the capabilities themselves.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is how much of that gap comes from deployment taking time, and how much comes from something missing in the models themselves. Those are very different explanations.

An evaluation gives you a question, and usually there is some way to determine whether the answer is correct. Real work can require you to figure out what the question should be. You have an unclear objective, incomplete information, and you need to make a sequence of decisions. If you make a mistake, you need to notice it and recover. Being very good at answering a difficult question doesn’t necessarily give you all of those abilities.

There is also a possibility that we are getting unusually good at the things we can measure. If you can measure a capability, you can put a lot of effort into improving it. But then you have to ask: how much did the underlying ability improve, and how much did performance improve in the particular circumstances of the test? You would want to distinguish those experimentally.

And economic impact introduces another layer. Suppose a model can do a task, but someone has to spend a comparable amount of time checking its work. That capability may be impressive while producing relatively little value. Reliability matters a great deal here.

So I would want to look closely at the failures. Does the model lack some knowledge? Does it misunderstand the objective? Does it fail to correct itself? The aggregate benchmark score hides these distinctions, and those distinctions may explain why the capability is difficult to turn into useful work.

sol-6.text: I think evaluations measure something real, but they often measure the model at its best on a well-defined task. In the real world, the task is rarely well defined. You need to understand what someone actually wants, work across many steps, notice when you’ve made a mistake, and recover. A small error rate that looks acceptable on a benchmark can become a serious problem when you depend on the system for an entire workflow. And economic impact takes time: people have to learn where these systems are reliable and change how they work. So I would take the evaluation results seriously, while also taking the gap seriously. It tells us that making models more capable and making them reliably useful are related, but they are not quite the same problem.

terra-5.6.text:
I think the main issue is reliability. A model can look extremely capable on short, well-specified evaluations, but real work is long-horizon, ambiguous, and full of opportunities to make a small mistake that compounds. People can notice when they are confused, recover, and keep working; current models often cannot do that robustly enough.

So the benchmarks are measuring something real, but they are not measuring the whole thing required for economic usefulness. As models become more reliable, can reason and act over longer horizons, and can learn from their experience, I expect that gap to shrink quite dramatically.

sol-5.6.text:
I think the key distinction is between doing a well-specified task and operating successfully in the messy real world. On an evaluation, the problem has already been formulated for the model: the relevant context is provided, the objective is clear, and success can usually be recognized immediately. In real work, much of the difficulty lies precisely in deciding what the problem is, gathering the right information, dealing with ambiguity, and sustaining a coherent course of action over a long period of time.

Current models are also uneven. They can produce something extremely impressive and then make a simple mistake. That unreliability matters much more economically than it does on a benchmark. If a system is correct 95 percent of the time, it may score very well, but if a human must carefully check every output, the amount of labor it actually replaces can be small.

There are organizational frictions too. Companies have existing processes, software, regulations, and incentives. Even when a model has the relevant cognitive ability, turning that ability into a dependable product takes time. So I would not interpret the gap as evidence that the evaluations are meaningless. I would interpret it as evidence that capability is only one ingredient. Reliability, long-horizon agency, access to the right context, and integration into the world are separate problems. If those improve, the economic impact could arrive quite suddenly, because a great deal of latent capability is already there.

luna-5.6.text:
I think the main issue is that evaluations measure capability in a very compressed, artificial setting, while the real world demands reliability over long horizons. A model can produce an impressive answer on a benchmark and still fail when the problem is ambiguous, when it has to ask the right questions, use tools, maintain context, or recover from an error. Those failures are disproportionately costly in real applications.

There’s also an integration gap. Economic impact doesn’t come from intelligence by itself; it comes from putting that intelligence into workflows, organizations, and products, with the necessary verification and accountability. Companies are understandably reluctant to delegate important decisions to systems that are occasionally brilliant and occasionally inexplicably wrong. So the models may be much more capable than current economic statistics suggest, but turning that capability into dependable labor is a separate and very difficult engineering problem.

luna-6.text:
I think the gap comes from the fact that an evaluation usually gives the model a very clean problem. You tell it exactly what to do, provide the relevant context, and then score the answer. In the real world, a lot of the work is figuring out what the problem is, gathering the right information, and carrying the task through reliably over time.

A model can be very capable on a particular step and still be hard to trust with the whole process. It might make a small mistake, lose track of an assumption, or need a person to check its work. And in many jobs, the cost of that supervision matters as much as how good the model is when it gets things right.

There’s also a deployment gap. Organizations have to change their workflows, connect systems, and decide who is accountable when something goes wrong. So strong evaluations tell us that useful capabilities are there, but they don’t automatically tell us how much work can be handed over, or how quickly that will happen. The economic impact depends on making the systems dependable enough and fitting them into real processes.
